title: New PR for Fixes minimal d-separator function failing to handle cases where no d-separators exist
description:
I couldn't push a rebase to PR #6438 (permission denied even though the branch allows maintainers to submit. perhaps because fork was originally not from networkx/networkx but I'm not sure why). So....

I have made a new PR with a rebased version of #6438.  @jaron-lee if you would like to pull this branch into your branch that might work. Otherwise we can use this new PR to continue the discussion from the old one. All the commits should still give attribution to @jaron-lee.

Fixes #6430 

For completeness, the original post was:

>Fixes https://github.com/networkx/networkx/issues/6430.

>Implement a check to verify the candidate minimal d-separator set is in fact a valid d-separating set
Added test to verify the function now returns None if there are no valid d-separating sets
Updated release_dev.rst to indicate changed API behavior
Updated documentation as required

comments.author: jaron-lee
comments.body:
Thanks for that. Happy to introduce renaming and testing around the `i` and `r` issue. API names should be easy on my end. 

Regarding the use of the inputs `i` and `r`, looking at the algorithm you definitely can't replicate removing `i` through passing a different graph (as this would require the moralization and subgraph operations to commute, which they don't). You also need to keep `r` - if you pass a subgraph of the original graph you risk removing certain paths, possibly leading you to conclude that you have a minimal separating set when in fact it might not separate at all (or perhaps no such set exists).

The use case for the `i` set being non-empty is if we want to find a minimal separating set that includes all vertices in `i`. Perhaps we have some reason to require conditioning on `i`, and want to know the minimal additional vertices to condition on for a separating set. Note that in this case we might end up with a larger minimal separating set compared to if `i` was empty (since not conditioning on `i` could leave certain paths closed due to colliders). It's a fairly niche use but I figured it's in the algorithm already and it would be more work to try and take it out correctly.

Similarly for `r` - maybe you want to consider only all separating sets of certain variables (and don't want to condition on certain other variables). However you'd still need to include these variables in the graph since this affects d-separatedness.

I'll have some time this week to try and close this out.

comments.author: Alex-Markham
comments.body:
>
>     * Couldn't you just take the union of the resulting separating set with `i` to make a separating set that includes `i`?
> 

It's a bit more complicated than that, because conditioning on nodes can open paths that would otherwise be blocked. For example, in the DAG `A -> B <- C -> D`, a minimal separating set between `A` and `D` is the empty set. If `i` is the singleton `{B}`, simply unioning that with the empty separating set renders `A` and `D` connected. Instead, the minimal separating set including `{B}` must be `{B, C}`.

comments.author: dschult
comments.body:
Continuing the name discussion:

I'd like all the different grammatical versions of "separate" to be the same within our function names. Otherwise, as a user, I would/will be constantly wondering which ending to put on my function name and inevitably getting it wrong and then having to look it up.

**What do people think about these function signatures?**
`find_d_minimal_separator(G, x, y, z, *, included=None, restricted=None)`
`is_d_separator(G, x, y, z)`
`is_minimal_d_separator(G, x, y, z, *, included=None, restricted=None)`

Why?
`find_minimal_d_separator` is better vs `find_minimal_d_separated` (we are finding the separator, not finding that they are separated)
`is_d_separator` seems to make sense -- we are checking if `z` is the separator. `is_d_separated` also works, but refers to the sets u, v being separated instead of z being the separator. I think either works fine, but separator matches the other names.
`is_minimal_d_separator`  could replace `minimal_d_separated`. I think we need the `is_` here to show it is a boolean return value. And either separator or separated works, but refer to the set z as separator vs the sets u, v being separated. 

For input names, I went back to look at what we currently use and I looked at the references. The current functions focus on u and v being nodes. Letting them be sets is an extra feature, but not currently supported. That's why they are named u and v (names we commonly use for nodes in networkx). `z` is not commonly used for nodes or sets in networkx and maybe could be called `separator`. But the references by Pearl and by Koller both consistently use x, y to denote the nodes or sets being separated and use z for the separator. So, I am currently in favor of the x, y, z formulation.

In terms of backward compatibility, my proposal above has two new function names and one existing name. The two old ones can be deprecated when the new ones are introduced. And hopefully the third has sufficiently similar output/logic to allow us not to deprecate. 

I haven't investigated the new failing tests @Alex-Markham talks about. But I am hopeful that either a bug will be identified or the new algorithm mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/pull/6438#issuecomment-1441113573) might pass all tests. I haven't even looked at that paper closely.

I'll try to pull the changes @Alex-Markham made so we can see them diffed and tested.

review_comments.author: rossbar
review_comments.body:
This is a high-level API comment, but my inclination is to *not* provide the "convenience" of passing in either nodes or a set of nodes. This case isn't quite as bad as other instances (i.e. the ambiguity of `str` being a sequence but also often representing a node; or the issue of tuples being both interpretable as nodes or sequences of nodes); but my general feeling is that type overloading in the API "for convenience" more often leads to ambiguity and corner cases.

A concrete example in this case might be if someone passed in a `frozenset` *with the intention that it be interpreted as a set of nodes*. The current pattern relies on the user knowing that `frozenset` does not inherit from `set` and thus would be treated as a node. In some sense this feels like a potential violation of duck-typing (`frozensets` quack like `sets`). OTOH - maybe this is what we want since `frozensets` are hashable and thus can also be nodes in a graph...

Anyways - not a blocker, but my feeling is that it'd be best to eschew the internal wrapping of inputs as sets based on type, especially since it doesn't actually save much typing on the part of the user (e.g. `y=3` becomes `y={3}`).

review_comments.author: dschult

Yes -- I agree that this is not the way to handle the input. And I don't like the idea of restricting it to only objects of type "set".  "frozenset" should be just as good -- as should lists, dict-keys, etc.  -- it's much better to have any container of nodes.  But, I also think it is nice to be flexible in accepting inputs.  This is a partial `nbunch` in that it allows a single node or a container of nodes. 

[Edited based on discussion with others] I propose that the check should convert any node in the graph to a set, but otherwise leave the input as it is.
```python
    x = {x} if x in G else x
```

+The intuition is as follows. The edges on a causal graph indicate which nodes
+influence the outcome of other nodes directly. An edge from u to v
+implies that the outcome of event ``u`` influences the probabilities for
+the outcome of event ``v``. Certainly knowing ``u`` changes predictions for ``v``.
+But also knowing ``v`` changes predictions for ``u``. The outcomes are dependent.
+Furthermore, an edge from ``v`` to ``w`` would mean that ``w`` and ``v`` are dependent
+and thus that ``u`` could indirectly influence ``w``.

+Without any knowledge about the system (candidate d-separating set is empty)
+a causal graph ``u -> v -> w`` allows all three nodes to be dependent. But
+if we know the outcome of ``v``, the conditional probabilities of outcomes for
+``u`` and ``w`` are independent of each other. That is, once we know the outcome
+for ```v`, the probabilities for ``w`` do not depend on the outcome for ``u``.
+This is the idea behind ``v`` blocking the path if it is "known" (in the candidate
+d-separating set).
+
+The same argument works whether the direction of the edges are both
+left-going and when both arrows head out from the middle. Having a "known"
+node on a path blocks the collider-free path because those relationships
+make the conditional probabilities independent.
+
+The direction of the causal edges does impact dependence precisely in the
+case of a collider e.g. ``u -> v <- w``. In that situation, both ``u`` and ``w``
+influence ``v```. But they do not directly influence each other. So without any
+knowledge of any outcomes, ``u`` and ``w`` are independent. That is the idea behind
+colliders blocking the path. But, if ``v`` is known, the conditional probabilities
+of ``u`` and ``w`` can be dependent. This is the heart of Berkson's Paradox [6]_.
+For example, suppose ``u`` and ``w`` are boolean events (they either happen or do not)
+and ``v`` represents the outcome "at least one of ``u`` and ``w`` occur". Then knowing
+``v`` is true makes the conditional probabilities of ``u`` and ``w`` dependent.

+probability of ``u`` to either the original value or 1. So the conditional
+probability of ``u`` depends on the outcome of ``w`` even though there is no
+causal relationship between them. When a collider is known, dependence can
+occur across paths through that collider. This is the reason open colliders
+do not block paths.
